checks.claim: Key: truck (20m at 0.5 m/s) and cyclist (m at 10 m/s) carry equal momentum (10m each), and the same steady force removes momentum at the same rate (change in momentum = force x time), so they stop in the same time
checks.note: OpenStax: 'Change in momentum equals the average net external force multiplied by the time this force acts.' Equal momentum, equal force, equal time. The idealisation (braking force is the whole net force, no drag) is fine at this level.

checks.claim: Momentum is mass times velocity (vector)
Wrong: 'The truck, since its mass is far greater' (mass alone does not set stopping time)
checks.note: Truly wrong: only the product mass x velocity matters for time under a given force.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The cyclist, since his speed is far greater'
checks.note: Truly wrong for the same reason.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The cyclist, since his energy is far greater' (energy sets stopping distance, not time)
checks.note: KE = 1/2 m v^2: cyclist 50m, truck 2.5m, ratio 20. Work-energy theorem (work = force x distance) makes the cyclist brake over 20 times the distance; HyperPhysics (https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/truckc2.html) gives the same equal-momentum comparison: the lighter, faster vehicle has more KE and needs more force to stop in a given distance. Time is still equal.

checks.claim: Context: cyclist has 20 times the energy, rolls 20 times as far, but for no longer
checks.note: Same time, average speeds 5 m/s vs 0.25 m/s: distance ratio 20. Arithmetic checked.

checks.claim: Context: at the bike's speed the truck would carry 20 times the momentum and need 20 times as long to stop
Key: no violation; the cloth's friction is an outside force, and total momentum is kept only with no net outside force
checks.note: OpenStax: 'Conservation of momentum is violated only when the net external force is not zero.'

checks.claim: A cue ball striking an equal ball squarely stops dead and the struck ball leaves with its speed (stop shot)
checks.note: Dr Dave Alciatore: 'the CB stops and the OB moves away with the original CB speed' (with stun, no spin, ideal collision). The stem gives the stop as observed, so no spin caveat is needed.

checks.claim: Context: in the split-second hit, friction is too small to matter, so the struck ball leaves with all the cue ball's momentum
checks.note: Dr Dave: momentum is conserved in the hit because no (significant) external forces act on the balls during it.

checks.claim: Context: afterwards friction passes the momentum to the table and Earth, too massive to be seen to move
checks.note: OpenStax's goalpost example: Earth recoils, 'immeasurably small'. Calling the cloth's rolling resistance 'friction' is fine at this grade.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'No, since the momentum has all turned into heat'
checks.note: Truly wrong: kinetic energy, not momentum, becomes heat; momentum passes to the Earth.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'No, since a still ball keeps its momentum stored'
checks.note: Truly wrong: a body at rest has zero momentum (mass x zero velocity).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Yes, since total momentum can never change at all'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the law holds only with no net external force.

checks.claim: Context: it is the ball's energy of motion, not its momentum, that ends up as heat
Key: held tight, his body and the rifle move back as one mass, so the recoil speed is small
checks.note: A Moment of Science: holding it tight, 'you make your body and the rifle act as one unit'; the combined mass recoils slowly. Same answer as the textbook problem in Wolfson's Essential University Physics.

checks.claim: Context: total momentum before the shot is zero; the rifle's backward momentum balances the bullet's and the gases' forward momentum
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the total momentum before and after the expulsion remains zero'; gases carry a large share.

checks.claim: Context: held loosely, the light rifle alone picks up speed and then strikes the shoulder hard
checks.note: Chuck Hawks: 'pull the rifle firmly against your shoulder'; 'Do not let it get a running start at you'; holding a hard-kicking rifle away from the shoulder can cause severe bruising.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'His grip cancels out the momentum of the kick'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the momentum is shared by a larger mass, not cancelled.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'His grip makes the kick last a shorter time'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the tight hold spreads the push over a longer time; the loose rifle's running start ends in a short, sharp hit.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The bullet leaves with less momentum than before' (bullet momentum same both times)
checks.note: Same rifle and load: the bullet's momentum is set by the cartridge, not the hold.

checks.claim: Key: she (half his mass) glides off faster, with as much momentum as he has
checks.note: schoolphysics: '0 = mv1 + mv2'; 'If the mass of the man is double that of the girl she will recoil at twice his speed'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'She does, with more momentum than he has'
checks.note: Truly wrong: momenta are equal and opposite (total stays zero).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'He does, since he gives the harder push' (third law: equal forces)
checks.note: Truly wrong: each pushes the other with an equal and opposite force at the same moment.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Neither, since they glide off equally fast'
checks.note: Truly wrong: equal speeds only with equal masses; the lighter skater moves faster.

checks.claim: Context: each pushes just as hard for the same moment, so the momenta match
checks.note: Illinois PHYS101 worked example: equal force for equal time gives equal and opposite impulses.

checks.claim: Descartes, Principles of Philosophy (1644): total quantity of motion, size times speed, is conserved
checks.note: SEP: the conserved quantity is 'the combined sum of the products of size and speed'; size roughly tracks volume.

checks.claim: Counted Descartes's way (scalar), two clay lumps that stop have lost their motion
checks.note: SEP: his quantity correlates with the scalar 'speed'; 'reversing the direction of B's motion does not alter the total quantity of motion'. Wikipedia: he believed speed rather than velocity is conserved.

checks.claim: Stem: 'Christiaan Huygens found a count that is kept in every collision'
checks.note: Wikipedia (Christiaan Huygens) says 'for all bodies' and Grokipedia 'conserved in all collisions', but Huygens's 1669 rules treat hard (elastic) bodies: the directional rule is listed 'as a characteristic of the collision of hard bodies' (arXiv 2512.22842), translations read 'the quantity of motion that two hard bodies have...', and the soft-body theory of 1668 was Wallis's (Oeuvres de Huygens XVI, https://www.dbnl.org/tekst/huyg003oeuv16_01/huyg003oeuv16_01_0006.php). Fix: 'Christiaan Huygens found a count, worked out for hard bodies, that is kept in these lumps too.' (or 'that is kept in collisions, and it holds for these lumps too').

checks.claim: Key: Huygens's count took the direction of motion into account
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'the conservation of quantity of motion in one direction'; Grokipedia: 'Huygens emphasized directional conservation'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The square of each body's speed'
checks.note: Truly wrong for the stem's case: mass x speed squared (Huygens's second rule) is kept only for hard bodies; in the clay collision it falls to zero.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The heat each collision gives off' and 'The push each body gives the other'
checks.note: Neither is part of Huygens's quantity.

checks.claim: Context: plus one and minus one before, nothing after: the quantity was kept
checks.note: Equal and opposite momenta sum to zero before and after a perfectly inelastic stick.

checks.claim: Context: 'Huygens also found that mass times the square of the speed adds up the same in collisions of hard, bouncing bodies, but not of soft ones like clay, which turn their motion into heat.'
checks.note: The hard-body half is right (Huygens's rule: the sum of each hard body's size times the square of its speed is the same before and after). But the sentence makes Huygens the finder of the soft-body failure and of heat: his rules dealt only with hard bodies (soft ones were Wallis's), and motion turned into heat is 19th-century physics. 'Turn their motion into heat' also blurs the very point of the question: the motion count (momentum) is kept; it is energy of motion that becomes heat. Fix: 'Huygens also found that mass times the square of the speed adds up the same when hard, bouncing bodies collide; it does not for soft ones like clay, which, as was learned much later, turn energy of motion into heat.'

checks.claim: Context: his directed count, mass times velocity, is now called momentum
Wren gave his theory of collisions to the Royal Society in 1668 (read 17 December 1668), printed with Wallis's in Phil. Trans., January 1669
Huygens's tract on impact read at the Royal Society on 7 January 1669
checks.note: Sent with his letter of 4 January 1669; read 7 January 1669; extract in Journal des Scavans 18 March 1669.

checks.claim: Wren and Huygens treated hard (elastic) bodies, Wallis soft (inelastic) ones
checks.note: Oeuvres de Huygens XVI: Wren's rules for perfectly hard bodies are identical to Huygens's; 'L'envoi de Wallis contient la theorie moderne du choc des corps mous.' Wallis's paper was read 26 November 1668.

checks.claim: Newton tested with pendulums of ten feet on strings, equal and unequal bodies, reading speed from the chord of the arc, 'without an error of 3 inches'
checks.note: Scholium: 'pendulums of ten feet, in unequal as well as equal bodies'; 'suspended by the parallel and equal strings'; velocity 'as the chord of the arc'; 'without an error of 3 inches'.

checks.claim: Balls of steel, glass, cork and wound wool; steel sprang apart almost as fast as they met, wool at little over half (5 to 9)
checks.note: 'balls of wool, made up tightly, and strongly compressed' (Latin conglomerata, wound into a ball); 'as about 5 to 9'; 'Balls of steel returned with almost the same velocity: those of cork with a velocity something less; but in balls of glass ... about 15 to 16'.

checks.claim: Key: the total momentum stayed the same for every kind of ball
checks.note: Newton: equal changes toward contrary parts, and the experiments 'do succeed as well in soft as in hard bodies'; the wool-ball predictions agreed. He gives only the rebound ratios for steel, cork and glass, but his general conclusion covers them. Acceptable.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'only for the steel balls'; 'only for equal-sized balls'; 'It shrank in the pairs that sprang apart slowly'
checks.note: All truly wrong: soft as well as hard; unequal as well as equal bodies; the slow rebound changes only the bounce.

checks.claim: Context quote 'as well in soft as in hard bodies'
checks.note: Verbatim in the Scholium (Motte 1846).

checks.claim: Context: a soft collision loses energy of motion to heat and squashing, never momentum
John Paul Stapp, an Air Force doctor
checks.note: Career USAF officer, flight surgeon and physician.

checks.claim: Rode Sonic Wind No. 1 in New Mexico in December 1954 to learn what a body can survive
checks.note: 10 December 1954, Holloman AFB, New Mexico. Smithsonian (https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/record-breaking-rocket-sled-created-modern-safety-standards): he was studying the effects of acceleration and deceleration on the human body.

checks.claim: 632 mph from a standstill in five seconds; stopped in 1.4 seconds
checks.note: Wikipedia (citing Aviation Week): 632 mph in five seconds, coasted half a second, stopped in 1.4 s. Popular Science agrees. NASA's history gives 937 ft/s (about 639 mph); the 632 figure is the standard one.

checks.claim: Key: the stop, which changed his speed in the least time, pressed hardest
checks.note: Same change of speed in 1.4 s against 5 s; the stop put 'a force of nearly four tons' on him (Smithsonian).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The start, when the rockets drove him forward hard'
checks.note: Truly wrong: average about 6 g over 5 s (Grokipedia gives about 20 g at most during acceleration), well below the stop.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The top speed, when he was moving at his fastest'
checks.note: Still wrong as the hardest, but not for the reason the context gives: the sled had 'no windshield at all', the run was designed 'to explore both deceleration and windblast', and wind pressure at top speed reached 7.7 psi. Consider 'The top speed, since speed itself presses on a body' so the lure names the misconception it is there for.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Start and stop alike, as both changed his speed equally'
checks.note: Truly wrong: equal change of momentum, very different times.

checks.claim: Context: the stop took a little over a quarter of the time
Context: the stop's force reached 46.2 g
checks.note: Wikipedia and Grokipedia give 46.2 g, the commonly cited figure. NASA's history reports a plateau of 25 g and over with peaks of 35 and 40 g, and Popular Science says 'more than 40 Gs'. The claim survives; 'more than 40 g' would be the safest wording.

checks.claim: Context: 'Moving fast at a steady speed presses on no one; only a change of speed does.'
checks.note: As a rule of inertia it is right, but it is said of this run, and on this run the wind pressed hard on him at top speed: NASA says 'no windshield at all was used', windblast reached 'as high as 7.7 pounds per square inch, or better than 1,100 pounds per square foot', and the run was designed to explore 'both deceleration and windblast'. Fix: 'Speed by itself presses on no one; only a change of speed does. (At top speed the wind did beat on him, since the sled had no windshield, but the stop pushed far harder.)' Or drop the sentence.

checks.claim: Context: textbooks of the day put 18 g as the limit of human tolerance
checks.note: Popular Science: 'Textbooks of the day put 18 Gs as the limit of human tolerance.' Paraphrase, not in quotation marks: fine.

checks.claim: Context: strapped into a strong harness, he lived through more than twice that
checks.note: Arms and legs secured, harness; 46.2 g (or NASA's 40 g peak) is more than 36 g.

checks.claim: Bela Barenyi, an engineer at Daimler-Benz
checks.note: Joined Daimler-Benz in 1939 as a body design engineer (Sindelfingen).

checks.claim: He doubted the long-held view that a safe car had to be rigid
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'Barenyi questioned the opinion that had prevailed until then that a safe car had to be rigid.'

checks.claim: Patent granted in 1952: stiff cabin between front and back built to crumple
checks.note: DRP No. 854 157, filed 23 January 1951, granted 28 August 1952; rigid passenger cell with deformable front and rear.

checks.claim: A 1959 Mercedes was the first car built to it
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'The first production implementation of crumple zones appeared in the Mercedes-Benz W111 series, introduced in 1959'; Wikipedia: first Mercedes-Benz carbody developed using the patent was the 1959 W111.

checks.claim: Key: crumpling makes the stop take longer, so the push on the people is gentler
checks.note: Benefit 'stems from the impulse-momentum theorem'; Wikipedia: average force 'inversely related to the time over which it is applied'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'less time, so the crash is over sooner'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the opposite.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It soaks up the car's momentum, so none of it reaches them'
checks.note: Truly wrong: it takes in energy by plastic deformation; the occupants still lose all their momentum.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It springs back, so the car rebounds'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the deformation is plastic, dissipated 'rather than rebound'.

checks.claim: Context: rigid car stops abruptly; crumpled metal stays crumpled taking in energy; the stiff cabin keeps its space
checks.note: 'Rigid vehicles stop abruptly, resulting in very high peak deceleration forces'.

checks.claim: Key: from the same height she meets the ground at the same speed and ends at rest, so the change in momentum is the same
Wrong: 'The force from the ground on her legs' (larger when stiff-legged)
checks.note: OpenStax: 'the force on your legs can be immense if you land stiff-legged on a hard surface'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The time it takes her to stop' and 'How sharply she slows to a stop'
checks.note: Truly wrong: bending the knees lengthens the time and lowers the deceleration; Grokipedia: 'athletes bending knees upon landing to minimize impact forces'.

checks.claim: Context: air bag, helmet foam and padded glove work the same way
checks.note: OpenStax: air bags let the force 'act over a much longer time', and 'giving' with a caught ball lowers the force; Grokipedia: the crushing EPS liner limits 'peak accelerations transmitted to the head'.

unit_notes: Physics of all nine items checks out; the two errors are in contexts (Q5's history sentence, Q7's 'presses on no one'). Q5's stem wording 'kept in every collision' credits Huygens with more than his hard-body rules said (uncertain; fix given). Q7: Stapp figures are the standard ones (632 mph, 5 s, 1.4 s, 46.2 g); NASA's own history gives peaks of 35 and 40 g and 937 ft/s, so 'more than 40 g' is the safest wording if the writer wants zero exposure.
